children.topic:
1. Definition &
Pathophysiology

Definition: Acute, reversible inflammatory process.
Pancreas can return to normal (unlike chronic)

Initial Event: Premature activation of
trypsinogen to trypsin inside acinar cells
Cascade of Autodigestion:

Trypsin activates elastase, collagenase,
phospholipase A2, lipase

Vascular Damage: Elastase/collagenase digest
blood vessels -> vasculitis, hemorrhage

Saponification: Lipase digests fat into fatty acids.
Binds calcium -> white chalky deposits.
Causes hypocalcemia (tetany)

SIRS: Necrosis attracts neutrophils -> cytokines.
Vasodilation, capillary leaks -> severe fluid
sequestration (third-spacing) and shock

Pulmonary Injury: Phospholipase A2 damages
surfactant -> left pleural effusion and ARDS

2. Etiology
(GET SMASHED)

G - Gallstones (40-50%): Most common cause.
Impaction at ampulla of Vater increases duct pressure

E - Ethanol / Alcohol (25-30%): Second most common.
Alters acinar cell permeability and vascularity
T - Tumors: Obstruction (e.g. pancreatic head cancer)
S - Scorpion stings
M - Mycoplasma or Mumps
A - Autoimmune: SLE or Polyarteritis Nodosa

S - Surgery or Trauma: Direct laceration
(steering wheel compression)

H - Hyperlipidemia / Hypercalcemia: Triglycerides > 1000 mg/dL.
Can cause pseudohyponatremia

E - ERCP or Embolic: 3% risk post-ERCP.
Prophylaxis: indomethacin rectal suppository

D - Drugs / Toxins: Furosemide, thiazides,
sulfasalazine, 5-ASA, azathioprine, valproic acid, exenatide

Idiopathic (20%): Often suspected biliary mud
(microscopic crystals)

3. Clinical Presentation
& Physical Signs

Pain (Prominent Feature): Sudden, severe epigastric pain
radiating straight to the back
Exacerbated by lying flat
Relieved by leaning forward

Associated Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting (90%),
anorexia, low-grade fever (60%)
Physical Exam:
General: Tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, cold sweats
Local: Mild epigastric tenderness, localized guarding, reactive ileus
Ecchymotic Signs (~5%): Retroperitoneal hemorrhage tracking
Cullen’s Sign: Blue-red periumbilical discoloration
Grey Turner’s Sign: Blue-black bilateral flank bruising
Fox’s Sign: Bruising over inguinal ligament

4. Diagnostic Criteria
(Atlanta Criteria)
Requires 2 out of 3 criteria:
1. Sudden, severe epigastric pain radiating to back
2. Serum Lipase or Amylase >= 3 times upper limit of normal

Lipase (100% Sensitive): Diagnostic test of choice.
Remains elevated for 10-14 days

Amylase (70% Sensitive): Elevated for only 2-3 days.
Extremely high amylase or ALT >3 times normal suggests gallstones
Pitfall: Magnitude of elevation does NOT correlate with severity
3. Characteristic findings on cross-sectional abdominal imaging

5. Imaging &
Workup

RUQ Ultrasound: Initial imaging of choice.
Rules out gallstones/biliary etiology
Abdominal X-ray:
Sentinel Loop: Dilated loop of small bowel in LUQ

Colon Cutoff Sign: Distension of proximal transverse colon
with collapse at splenic flexure

Chest X-ray: Left-sided pleural effusion or atelectasis.
Strong marker of severity

Contrast-Enhanced CT: NOT mandatory on admission.
Gold standard for evaluating necrosis, fluid collections, abscess

Indications: Doubtful diagnosis, failure to improve
after 3 days, or suspected sepsis

6. Severity Classification
& Prognosis
Atlanta Severity Classification:
Mild (80-90%): No organ failure/complications. Resolves 2-5 days
Moderately Severe: Transient organ failure (< 48 hours)
Severe: Persistent organ failure (> 48 hours). Worst prognosis
Cardiovascular: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg despite hydration
Respiratory: PaO2 <= 60 mmHg
Renal: Creatinine > 2.0 mg/L after resuscitation
GI: Severe bleeding > 500 cc/24 hours
Ranson’s Criteria: 0-2 pts = 2% mortality, >6 pts = 100%

On Admission (GA LAW): Glucose >200, Age >55, LDH >350,
AST >250, WBC >16,000

At 48 Hours (CHOBBS): Calcium 10%,
PaO2 =5, Base deficit >4, Sequestration >6 L

BISAP Score: BUN >25, Impaired mental status,
SIRS criteria, Age >60, Pleural effusion

7. Conservative Management
(The 6 "R"s)

1. Replacement of Fluids: Aggressive IV crystalloids.
Goal: urine output >= 0.5 cc/kg/hr

2. Relief of Pain: Pethidine (meperidine) traditionally
preferred over morphine to avoid sphincter of Oddi spasm
3. Rest of Pancreas & Bowel: Strictly NPO

If NPO >7 days: Enteral nutrition via nasojejunal tube
preferred over TPN (maintains barrier, prevents infection)

4. Respiratory Support: Oxygen mask or mechanical
ventilation with PEEP if ARDS

5. Resistance of Infection: Routine prophylactic antibiotics
NOT recommended

Imipenem reserved for infected necrotizing pancreatitis
or pancreatic abscess
6. Reassessment: Continuous monitoring and repeat CT

Mild Gallstone Pancreatitis: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
during same admission (within 48-72 hrs)

Severe Pancreatitis: Delay cholecystectomy for weeks
until inflammation resolves

8. Locorregional
Complications
A. Pancreatic Abscess / Infected Necrosis:
Pathophysiology: Bacterial translocation across gut wall (3-4 weeks)
Picture: New fever, leukocytosis, instability after initial resolution
Diagnostics: CT scan shows necrotic tissue with gas bubbles

Treatment (Step-Up): 1. Imipenem based on FNA culture.
2. Percutaneous drainage. 3. VARD. 4. Open necrosectomy
B. Pancreatic Pseudocyst (10% of cases):
Definition: Fluid/enzymes in fibrous capsule lacking epithelial lining
Pathogenesis: Develops 2-3 weeks later in lesser sac (omental bursa)

Presentation: 4-6 weeks later, vague pain, early satiety,
palpable epigastric mass, elevated amylase
Rule of 6 (Indications for Drainage):
Duration > 6 weeks, Diameter > 6 cm, Wall thickness > 6 mm
Or complications: Infection, rupture, splenic artery pseudoaneurysm
Management:
First-Line: Internal Drainage (Cystogastrostomy or Cystojejunostomy)
Contraindicated: External drainage (causes difficult fistulas)
